sources.citation: Hellenic Ministry of Culture and Sports, Odysseus portal: Archaeological site of Aphaia, Aigina (Description).
sources.quote: It is situated on the top of a hill covered with pines, in the NE part of the island, and is distinguished by the very good preservation of the Late Archaic temple. The sanctuary was initially dedicated to the cult of Aphaia, a local deity later assimilated by Athena.
sources.note: Reachable over http:// only (the https host refused connections). Further quotable line: "At the end of the period, around 500 B.C. and a little later, the sanctuary assumed the monumental form it preserves today." The page gives no dimensions and does not describe the pediments.

sources.citation: Hellenic Ministry of Culture and Sports, Odysseus portal: Archaeological site of Aphaia, Aigina (History).
sources.quote: The first systematic archaeological investigation was begun in 1901 by the German Ad. Furtwaengler. Work was resumed in 1966 by the German D. Ohly, who excavated on the site until 1979 and was continued by his collaborators until 1988.
sources.note: Reachable over http:// only. The same tab records the removal of the pediment sculptures in 1811 and their display in the Glyptothek, Munich.

sources.citation: Pausanias, Description of Greece 2.30.3, trans. W. H. S. Jones and H. A. Ormerod (Loeb Classical Library; Harvard University Press / Heinemann, 1918), via Perseus.
sources.quote: In Aegina, as you go towards the mountain of Zeus, God of all the Greeks, you reach a sanctuary of Aphaea, in whose honor Pindar composed an ode for the Aeginetans.
sources.licence: Translation public domain (1918). Perseus encodes it under a Creative Commons licence: confirm the exact licence before shipping.
sources.note: Same paragraph: "Her surname among the Aeginetans is Aphaea; in Crete it is Dictynna (Goddess of Nets)." Pausanias relates the Britomartis story but says nothing about the architecture or the pediments.

sources.citation: Pindar, ode composed for the Aeginetans in honour of Aphaia (lost; known through Pausanias 2.30.3).
sources.note: No text of the ode located. Furtwängler 1906 links Pindar's praise of the Aiakidai to the pediment subjects; that is interpretation, not a quotation.

sources.licence: The only translation found (F. Celoria, 1992) is copyrighted: paraphrase only, never quote it in the app.
sources.note: Britomartis flees Minos to Aegina; escaping a fisherman she vanishes into a grove, and the Aeginetans call her Aphaia. The 'she who disappeared' etymology is secondary and unconfirmed.

sources.citation: Furtwängler, A., E. R. Fiechter and H. Thiersch. Aegina: Das Heiligtum der Aphaia. Munich, 1906 (text volume).
sources.licence: Public domain (1906); digitised at the Internet Archive.
sources.note: Primary source for dimensions, polychrome observations and pediment compositions. Read as archive.org OCR; page numbers are the printed running heads. Plates not seen; Heidelberg copy not opened (bot-gated).

sources.note: Image-only PDF, no OCR text; nothing read directly. Cited only via Furtwängler 1906.

sources.note: Print-only. Nothing read. Stays verified:false with no page numbers unless the user supplies page scans.

sources.citation: Brinkmann, V., and U. Koch-Brinkmann. Gods in Color: research and reconstructions of ancient polychromy (Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung).
sources.note: Research objects include both Aphaia pediments, the archer in Scythian dress, an Athena and a warrior's head (Wikipedia, secondary). No Brinkmann text on the tympanum colour was read.

sources.citation: Harvard Gazette, "Scholars give us antiquity, the colorized version", September 2007.
sources.quote: The figure wears a shirt and leggings covered all over with an intricate red, yellow, blue, and green diamond pattern. Over this he wears a bright yellow vest inscribed with lions and griffins.
sources.note: On the west-pediment archer. Also: "A tall yellow hat with a flower pattern completes the costume." The curator says he "probably represents Paris".

sources.note: Not read (HTTP 429). Pigment list (Egyptian blue, red ochre with cinnabar, malachite, gold ochre, umber) known only from a search summary.

britomartis.note: Daughter of Zeus and Carme, fled Minos; worshipped in Aegina as Aphaia.

athena.note: Central figure of both pediments, unseen by the combatants (Furtwängler 1906, p. 310).

herakles.note: Helmeted archer with a lion-skin helmet front in the later east pediment (pp. 308-310). Which side he stands on is unverified.

telamon.note: With Herakles against Laomedon: the first Trojan War, subject of the later east pediment (pp. 312-314).

trojan-archer.term: Trojan archer (identified as Paris by some)
trojan-archer.note: Conflict: Furtwängler 1906 (p. 308) says the old name Paris rests on false assumptions; the 2007 Gods in Color curators say he probably represents Paris.

site-georeference.description: The temple frame is georeferenced for the real terrain: stylobate elevation 178.14 m (DERIVED: Copernicus DEM at the OSM temple centroid minus 1 m, +/-3 m) and axis true bearing 69.1 degrees (DERIVED from the OSM outline, +/-2 degrees).
site-georeference.note: Both values are derived, not surveyed (measurements/georef.json). The sea level in the frame follows: y = -178.14.

terrain-real-beyond-terraces.description: Beyond the terrace walls the real hill and coast from the Copernicus DEM are shown; inside, the c. 490 BC terrace surfaces at Furtwängler's levels. Where today's surface rises above an ancient terrace edge, a cut face is built and the mismatch is logged.

sanctuary-phase-c490.description: The sanctuary is shown as completed c. 490 BC (Late Archaic layout); older and later structures are listed but hidden.

propylon-stairs-south.description: The propylon's flight of steps rises from the south (outer) side, as the excavator describes it.
propylon-stairs-south.note: Conflict: the 2007 plan draws three step lines on the north (inner) side; Furtwängler pp. 75-77 puts the stair on the outer side, with the gutters draining over it outwards. Text followed (lead decision).

votive-column-shown.description: The sphinx votive column is always shown, flagged uncertain: it is 6th-century and only 'not impossibly' spared at the rebuilding.

suedbau-shown.description: The Südbau terrace south of the sanctuary is always shown, flagged uncertain; it is off the plan sheet and placed from the text distances.

sanctuary-terrain.description: Terrain around the terraces is a conjectural reconstruction from the text's levels (steep fall east and north, gentle west and south, Südbau about 9 m below the stylobate), not a survey; the scan covers only the temple.

polychrome-scheme.description: Architectural colours follow what the 1906 excavators observed on Aphaia itself; the sculpture follows the Gods in Color reconstructions; gaps are filled by analogy with other Archaic temples.

black-triglyphs-and-mutules.description: Triglyphs and mutules are black, not blue: fragments found on Aphaia show black; Cockerell's blue rests on an opisthodomos piece.

dimension-baseline.description: Absolute size is anchored to the published dimensions of Furtwängler et al. 1906; the scan verifies proportions.

flank-interaxial-2-57.description: Flank interaxial 2.57 m (two text statements, pp. 24 and 55) is used over 2.56 m (p. 52 table).

corner-contraction-p29.description: Corner contraction uses the measured values on p. 29 (east 0.25 m, south 0.245 m) over the garbled p. 55 figures.

no-curvature.description: The stylobate is built level, with no curvature ("Somit ist eine Kurvatur nicht vorhanden").

east-ramp.description: A stone ramp on the east front, slope 1:6, reaching the second step and leading on to the altar.
east-ramp.note: Ramp p. 25; slope in section II.1 (page not pinned).

east-pediment-displayed.description: The later east pediment (c. 480 BC, Herakles and Telamon against Laomedon) is displayed on a c. 500 BC temple.
east-pediment-displayed.note: User decision 2026-11-16. The earlier east pediment is known only indirectly.

pediment-figure-order.description: Left-to-right figure order (west A-N, east A-L) inferred from Furtwängler's group descriptions and lettering; no single page gives it.

archer-identity.description: The painted west-pediment archer is labelled "Trojan archer (identified as Paris by some)".
